  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Kathryn Bishop (E023) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write; admin requires the role to own the system (Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist), so write is the maximum. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):

  - employment type: contractor

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

The employee is Kathryn Bishop (E023), requesting write access to Payroll.

Two notes:
- Note 1 (HR-ish): role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommend write.
- Note 2 (Security): role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommend read. Security records disagree with HR note.

The policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system. Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist, Engineer doesn't own it. So full-time Engineer max = write. Requested write → grant write.
- contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Basic training → max read. Requested write → grant read.

The conflict: HR says full-time, Security says contractor with basic training.

Which to believe? The notes conflict. The security DB shows contractor with basic training. The recommendation from security is read.

As the Approver, I need to make a decision. Team memory contains conflicting notes. Typically, when there's a conflict between HR and Security records, security records tend to be more authoritative for access, or we should take the more restrictive. Contractor with basic training → max read.

Given conflicting info, the safer approach is to grant the lower level, since security records indicate contractor/basic training which caps at read. The requested level is write, max per security note is read, so grant read.

Alternatively, if full-time, write is allowed and grant write. But since records disagree, we choose the more restrictive/secure option: read.

I'll submit decision: read.
